Donuts and gauges

Both are drawn with a conic-gradient rather than SVG, so a slice is one custom property and nothing has to compute an arc path. Put data-value on the figure and the script does the rest.

Donut

68% Storage
94%
12%
4 Sources
Direct 45% Search 30% Referral 15% Social 10%

The hole is cut with a mask, not filled with a circle of the surface color, so the figure sits correctly on a sunken stage or a colored band. One consequence: a label cannot be a child of .donut, because the mask would cut that too — hence the separate .donut-center layered over it by .donut-figure.

Gauge

72 Capacity
0100
1,480 req/s
02,000
38 of 40 h
040

A gauge takes data-min and data-max, so the sweep is a proportion of the range rather than of a hundred — 1,480 out of 2,000 fills about three quarters of the arc.

info
Use these for one number, not for comparison Every radial form shares one flaw: an angle is much harder to judge than a length. A single figure in the middle of a donut reads well, because the number carries the value and the ring only decorates it. Six slices of similar size do not — nobody can tell 17% from 19% by eye at that size. When the point is to compare, a bar chart is the honest choice, and the legend above exists precisely because the ring alone cannot be read.

Each figure carries role="img" and a label naming the value, because a conic gradient says nothing to a screen reader and the text in the middle is a separate element that may not be read alongside it. Where reduced motion is preferred, the sweep is set at once instead of animating from zero.

Long lists

Three ways to show more rows than fit, in increasing order of cost. Reach for the cheapest one that works: pagination and a "load more" button need no observers and no measurement, and they are the only two where a reader can reliably get back to a row they saw a minute ago.

ApproachRight whenCosts
Pagination Rows are addressable and people come back to them. Nothing. A page number is a URL.
Load more Reading is linear and the list has an end in sight. One click per batch, and the footer keeps moving away.
Infinite scroll Browsing is casual and nobody needs to return to a row. The footer becomes unreachable, and the back button loses the position.
Windowing Thousands of rows have to exist at once in one scroller. Fixed row heights, no in-page search, and a scrollbar to keep honest.

Load more

Focus moves to the first newly revealed row, so the keyboard carries on where the eye does rather than jumping back to the top of the list.

Infinite scroll

An IntersectionObserver watches a sentinel below the last row. It disconnects at the end of the data, so an exhausted list stops costing anything — and the end gets a line saying so, because a list that simply stops producing rows is indistinguishable from one that broke.

Windowing

Ten thousand rows, of which about a dozen exist at any moment. A sizer carries the full height so the scrollbar stays honest, and the window of real rows is translated into position under the viewport.

warning

What windowing costs

A row that is not in the DOM cannot be found by the browser's own Ctrl+F, cannot be read by a screen reader walking the list, and cannot be printed. Rows also have to be a known fixed height. Do not window a list of a few hundred rows to save a few milliseconds — the trade is a bad one until the thousands.
